rows.note: In the ayah the verb commands recitation, and Biblical Hebrew קרא can mean reading aloud as well as calling or proclaiming.

rows.explanation: Moses reads the book of the covenant aloud to the people.
The king is to read the law throughout his life.
The law is to be read before all Israel.
Joshua reads the words of the law aloud.
Joshua reads everything Moses commanded before the assembly.
Shaphan reads the discovered book of the law.
Shaphan reads the book before the king.
Ezra reads from the law before the assembly.
The Levites read from the law and explain it.
The command to read from the book of the LORD uses קרא.
Baruch is told to read the scroll aloud.
Baruch reads Jeremiah’s words in the house of the LORD.
Calling upon the name of the LORD uses קרא בשם, a similar phrase with the sense of invocation.
Abram calls upon the name of the LORD rather than reading aloud.
Abram again calls upon the name of the LORD.
Abraham calls upon the name of the LORD.
Isaac calls upon the name of the LORD.
Elijah contrasts calling on the name of the LORD with calling on other gods.
The speaker calls upon the name of the LORD.
The speaker promises to call upon the name of the LORD.
The speaker repeats that promise to call upon the name of the LORD.

rows.note: In the ayah اسم means “name,” as does Biblical Hebrew שם.

rows.explanation: The name of the LORD is the object of the recurring invocation formula.
Abram calls upon the name of the LORD.
Abram again calls upon the name of the LORD.
Abraham calls upon the name of the LORD.
Isaac calls upon the name of the LORD.
David says he comes in the name of the LORD of hosts.
David blesses the people in the name of the LORD of hosts.
Elijah says he will call upon the name of the LORD.
Elijah builds an altar in the name of the LORD.
The speaker calls upon the name of the LORD.
The speaker calls upon the name of the LORD.
The speaker calls upon the name of the LORD.
The one who comes in the name of the LORD is blessed.
Help is in the name of the LORD, maker of heaven and earth.

rows.note: In the ayah رَبّ addresses God as Lord, whereas Biblical Hebrew רב denotes greatness or a human chief and Biblical Aramaic uses related forms for human lords.

rows.explanation: Each רַב of the king’s household is an officer rather than a divine lord.
רַב describes the greater or elder of two peoples, showing the sense of rank.
The Aramaic title רַב makes Daniel chief over the governors of the wise men.
The Aramaic title רַב calls Daniel chief of the magicians.
The Aramaic רַבְרְבָן denotes Belshazzar’s human lords.
The same Aramaic word again denotes Belshazzar’s lords.
The Aramaic רַב denotes a chief over the magicians.

rows.note: The ayah’s خَلَقَ means “created,” whereas the similarly sounding Hebrew חלק means “divided” or “apportioned.”
